subject: history
title: Henry VII and Henry VIII: Dynasty and Break with Rome
welcome_lead: Examine how Henry VII secured the Tudor dynasty and how Henry VIII's marital crisis shattered England's Roman allegiance.
meta_desc: AQA A-Level Tudors 1485-1603 adventure on Henry VII's consolidation and Henry VIII's break with Rome 1534.
final_note: You can now explain the dynastic and religious foundations of Tudor power.

concepts.def: Henry Tudor's defeat of Richard III on 22 August 1485, founding the Tudor dynasty.
Royal court under Henry VII used to enforce law against over-mighty subjects and curb retaining.
Financial sureties imposed by Henry VII to bind nobles to good behaviour and tighten royal control.
Statute drafted by Thomas Cromwell declaring England 'an empire' free from papal jurisdiction, enabling Henry's divorce.
Statute declaring Henry VIII Supreme Head of the Church of England, completing the legal break with Rome.
1536-40 closure of religious houses under Cromwell, transferring vast lands and wealth to the Crown.

walkthroughs.body_html: After Bosworth (1485), Henry VII faced pretenders Lambert Simnel (defeated at Stoke 1487) and Perkin Warbeck (executed 1499). He neutralised the nobility through bonds and recognisances, the Council Learned in the Law (Empson and Dudley), and Acts against retaining (1487, 1504). The Treaty of Medina del Campo (1489) secured the Spanish match; the Intercursus Magnus (1496) stabilised Burgundian trade. He left a solvent treasury.

walkthroughs.h2: Wolsey and the King's Great Matter
walkthroughs.body_html: Cardinal Wolsey dominated 1515-29 as Lord Chancellor, pursuing French wars and the Amicable Grant (1525) fiasco. Henry's quest to annul his marriage to Catherine of Aragon (the 'Great Matter') foundered on Pope Clement VII's dependence on Charles V after the 1527 Sack of Rome. Wolsey fell in 1529.

Thomas Cromwell drove statute through Parliament: the Act in Restraint of Appeals (1533) blocked Catherine's appeal to Rome; Cranmer annulled the marriage; the Act of Supremacy (1534) made Henry Supreme Head. The Treason Act (1534) criminalised denial of the supremacy (executions of More and Fisher 1535). The Dissolution (1536-40) yielded approximately £1.3 million and provoked the Pilgrimage of Grace (1536).
